blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Variance is the average squared deviation from the mean. The sum of squares (SS) is Σ(x − x̄)², the total of the squared deviations.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Squaring, like taking absolute values, stops positive and negative deviations cancelling. Squaring also weights large deviations more heavily, and it gives variance an algebra that absolute values lack: sums of squares split into meaningful parts. That property, shown below, underlies standard errors, ANOVA (literally “analysis of variance”, §9.5) and regression.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
For any number c, write x − c = (x − x̄) + (x̄ − c), square and add over all n values:

Σ(x − c)² = Σ(x − x̄)² + 2(x̄ − c)·Σ(x − x̄) + n(x̄ − c)²

The middle term is zero, because Σ(x − x̄) = 0 (recall §2.2.1). So

Σ(x − c)² = SS + n(x̄ − c)²

Two consequences follow. First, the sum of squared deviations is smallest when c = x̄: the mean is the centre that minimises squared distance, as the median minimises absolute distance (§3.5). Second, the total squared distance from any point splits exactly into “spread around the mean” plus “distance of the mean from that point”. No such split exists for absolute distances.

Check on the five children (x̄ = 11, SS = 10): about c = 12, Σ(x − 12)² = 9 + 4 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 15 = 10 + 5 × 1². Expanding the square the same way also gives the hand-computing formula SS = Σx² − (Σx)² ÷ n: here 615 − 55² ÷ 5 = 615 − 605 = 10.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Five weights 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, mean 11. Deviations −2, −1, 0, 1, 2; squared 4, 1, 0, 1, 4; SS = 10. Treating these five as the whole population, variance = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 kg².

points.html: Variance is in squared units (kg²), which is hard to picture. The standard deviation (§3.7) takes the square root to return to kg.
Two versions exist: the population variance divides SS by N (§3.6.1); the sample variance divides by n − 1 (§3.6.2).
Identity to remember: Σ(x − c)² = SS + n(x̄ − c)². It is the first instance of the partitioning of sums of squares that ANOVA and regression use.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Population variance (σ²) is the average squared deviation of every value in a population from the population mean μ: σ² = Σ(x − μ)² ÷ N.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: When every unit of the population is measured, μ is known exactly and nothing is estimated. Dividing by N gives the true average squared deviation.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: If you weighed all 50,000 under-five children in a district, summed their squared deviations from the district mean and divided by 50,000, you would have σ². It is one fixed number, a parameter (recall §1.3), even though nobody may ever compute it.

points.html: σ² = Σ(x − μ)² ÷ N. It is a parameter, written with a Greek letter.
Research almost never has the whole population, so σ² is estimated from a sample (§3.6.2).

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Sample variance (s²) estimates σ² from a sample of n values by dividing the sum of squares by n − 1: s² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1). Dividing by n − 1 instead of n is Bessel’s correction.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: In a sample you do not know μ, so you measure deviations from x̄. But x̄ was computed from the same values, and §3.6 showed that x̄ is the point that makes the sum of squared deviations smallest. Deviations from x̄ are therefore, as a rule, a little smaller than the deviations from μ that σ² is built on. Divide by n and you underestimate σ² on average over repeated samples; any single sample can still land above σ². Dividing by n − 1 enlarges the estimate by exactly the right amount, on average. The derivation shows why the factor is exactly n − 1.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Put c = μ in the identity from §3.6:

SS = Σ(x − μ)² − n(x̄ − μ)²

Now average both sides over all possible samples of n independently drawn values. (This long-run average over all possible samples is called the expected value, written E[·].)

  1. Each (x − μ)² averages σ², by the definition of σ². So E[Σ(x − μ)²] = nσ².
  2. x̄ − μ = (1/n)Σ(x − μ). Its square is (1/n²) × [Σ(x − μ)² + the cross-products (xᵢ − μ)(xⱼ − μ) for i ≠ j]. For independent draws, the average of a product is the product of the averages, and each deviation from μ averages 0, so every cross-product averages 0. Hence E[(x̄ − μ)²] = (1/n²) × nσ² = σ²/n. (Its square root, σ/√n, is the standard error of the mean, §6.7.)
  3. Therefore E[SS] = nσ² − n × σ²/n = (n − 1)σ².

So E[SS ÷ n] = (n − 1)σ²/n, which is too small, and E[SS ÷ (n − 1)] = σ². An estimator whose average over repeated samples equals the parameter is called unbiased (the formal definition is in §7.1.1): s² is unbiased for σ², and SS ÷ n is not.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: checking the derivation exactly
blocks.html:
Treat the five weights 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 as a whole population: μ = 11, σ² = 2 (§3.6). Draw samples of n = 2 children independently (with replacement). There are 5 × 5 = 25 equally likely ordered samples. For each, SS = Σ(x − x̄)²:

SS SS ÷ n (n = 2) SS ÷ (n − 1) Number of samples
0 0 0 5
0.5 0.25 0.5 8
2 1 2 6
4.5 2.25 4.5 4
8 4 8 2
  1. Average SS = (0×5 + 0.5×8 + 2×6 + 4.5×4 + 8×2) ÷ 25 = 50 ÷ 25 = 2, which equals (n − 1)σ² = 1 × 2.
  2. Average of SS ÷ n = 1: dividing by n gets σ² = 2 wrong by half, on average.
  3. Average of SS ÷ (n − 1) = 2 = σ²: Bessel’s correction is exactly right on average.
  4. Yet in 6 of the 25 samples (SS = 4.5 or 8), even SS ÷ n exceeds σ². The bias is a property of the average, not of every sample.

The same enumeration with n = 3 (125 samples) gives average SS ÷ n = 1.33 = (2/3) × 2, and average SS ÷ (n − 1) = 2 again.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: The five weights as a sample: SS = 10, so s² = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 kg², larger than the population-formula value of 2. For today’s 30 children, s² = 88.95 ÷ 29 = 3.07 kg².

points.html: s² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1), and E[Σ(x − x̄)²] = (n − 1)σ².
The divisor n − 1 is the degrees of freedom of s² (§3.6.3). The degrees-of-freedom story is intuition; the derivation above is the proof.
The correction matters in small samples (4 against 5 is a 25% difference) and hardly at all in large ones (999 against 1000).

s² is unbiased for σ², but s = √s² is not unbiased for σ: it underestimates σ slightly on average, because the square root of an average exceeds the average of square roots. In the n = 2 enumeration above, the average s is 1.13, against σ = √2 = 1.41.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Degrees of freedom (df) is the number of independent pieces of information left for estimating a quantity after the constraints already imposed on the data are counted: usually, the number of observations minus the number of parameters estimated from them first.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Once x̄ is calculated from n values, the n deviations from it must sum to zero (recall §2.2.1). Know any n − 1 of them and the last is fixed. So only n − 1 deviations are free to vary, and s² has n − 1 degrees of freedom. The derivation in §3.6.2 reaches the same n − 1 by algebra.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Five weights with mean 11. If four deviations are −2, −1, 0 and +1, the fifth must be +2 to make the sum zero. Only 4 of the 5 deviations carry new information; s² divides by 4.

points.html: General rule: df = number of independent observations − number of parameters estimated from them before the quantity in question.

df is not the sample size. The same dataset can give different df in different calculations, depending on how many parameters each had to estimate first. The same subtraction returns in the t-distribution (§5.7.2.3), the chi-square test (§10.6) and regression (Chapter 12).
